title: Preface
summary: Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K is its annual report for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2024. It identifies the company, incorporation, address, contact details, registered common stock and notes, and NYSE symbols. It reports filer status, filing and interactive-data compliance, internal-control attestation, shell-company status, market value and shares outstanding. It also notes that portions of the 2024 proxy statement are incorporated by reference into specified Form 10-K sections.

title: Walmart Inc. Form 10-K For the Fiscal Year Ended January 31, 2024
summary: Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2024 lists sections and page numbers covering business and risk factors; legal, cybersecurity, property, mine safety, and market disclosures; management’s discussion, market risk, and financial statements; accounting, controls, and other information; corporate governance, executive compensation, ownership, related-party matters, and audit fees; exhibits, financial statement schedules, a Form 10-K summary, and signatures.

title: ANNUAL REPORT ON FORM 10-K FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JANUARY 31, 2024
summary: Walmart Inc.’s Form 10-K covers the fiscal year ended January 31, 2024. References to the Company and related terms mean Walmart Inc. and, unless otherwise specified, its consolidated subsidiaries. The report notes that a 3-for-1 common stock split and proportional increase in authorized shares took effect February 23, 2024; all share and per-share information, including stock-based compensation, is retroactively adjusted.

title: PART I
summary: Walmart’s report explains that its filings, announcements and presentations may contain Exchange Act-protected forward-looking statements about future performance, plans and goals. Topics include economic and market conditions, business growth, financial and operating measures, investments, workforce, currency, shareholder returns, liquidity and cash flows, taxes, regulation, litigation, accounting standards, and ESG commitments. Such statements are identifiable by predictive language, rely on current knowledge and assumptions, and may differ materially from actual outcomes due to risks and uncertainties. They speak only as of their dates; Walmart cautions against undue reliance and disclaims any duty to update except as required by law.

title: ITEM 1. BUSINESS

nodes.title: The Development of Our Company
nodes.summary: Walmart describes itself as a people-led, technology-powered omnichannel retailer focused on saving customers money and time through stores, eCommerce and services. It serves about 255 million customers weekly across 10,500-plus stores and websites in 19 countries, guided by convenience, disciplined operations, digital growth and trust. Its EDLP pricing and EDLC cost controls support everyday low prices. Three segments are Walmart U.S., Walmart International and Sam’s Club; fiscal 2024 revenue was $648.1 billion, including $642.6 billion in net sales. The company is headquartered in Bentonville, trades as WMT, and reports fiscal years ending January 31 for U.S. and Canadian operations. Its history spans variety stores beginning in 1945, discount retail, public listing, Sam’s Club, supercenters, Neighborhood Markets, international expansion, and eCommerce launched in 2000. It highlights pickup and delivery networks, Flipkart and PhonePe investments, approximately 2.1 million associates, Walmart+ and expansion into advertising, marketplaces, fulfillment, healthcare and financial services.

nodes.title: Information About Our Segments
nodes.summary: The company operates retail, wholesale, other and eCommerce businesses across the U.S., Africa, Canada, Central America, Chile, China, India and Mexico; it sold its U.K. and Japan operations in the first quarter of fiscal 2022. Its three reportable segments are Walmart U.S., Walmart International and Sam’s Club, each contributing differently but generally consistently to net sales. International’s contribution has shifted slightly due to market exits and currency fluctuations. Further details on divestitures and segment and geographic information are in Notes 12 and 13, respectively, to the Consolidated Financial Statements.

nodes.title: Walmart U.S. Segment
nodes.summary: The text describes Walmart U.S. and Walmart International, covering their markets, formats, fiscal 2024 sales and historical performance; store sizes and omni-channel services, including memberships, pickup, delivery, eCommerce and digital platforms; merchandise categories, private and licensed brands, and related advertising, fulfillment, health, data and financial services; operating practices and seasonality; competition, competitive pressures and strategies; and distribution networks and fulfillment methods. It also outlines International’s countries, ownership and recent portfolio changes, local-market strategy, and regional offerings.

nodes.title: Sam's Club Segment
nodes.summary: Sam’s Club operates U.S. warehouse clubs and e-commerce, reporting fiscal 2024–2022 sales and relying significantly on membership income. The text describes membership tiers, fees, benefits and Sam’s Cash; omnichannel services, club sizes, operating technology and hours; five merchandise categories and the Member’s Mark brand; seasonality and competition; and distribution facilities and shipping. It also covers the company’s intellectual-property protections and licensing, global supplier relationships and supply-chain factors affecting availability and assortment, and exposure to U.S. and foreign laws and regulations.

nodes.title: Sam’s Club Operations, Intellectual Property and Risks
nodes.summary: Sam’s Club describes its merchandise assortment and expanding Member’s Mark brand, member services and technology, seasonal sales patterns, competition, and distribution and fulfillment network. The page also covers protection and licensing of intellectual property; its global supplier relationships, supplier standards, and supply-chain effects on product availability and assortment; and exposure to U.S. and foreign laws and regulations, with related risks discussed elsewhere.

nodes.title: Environmental, Social and Governance ("ESG") Priorities
nodes.summary: Walmart’s ESG strategy seeks shared value and long-term competitive advantage by addressing issues relevant to its business and stakeholders, building trust, opportunities, capabilities, and resilience while managing cost and risk. Its priorities span four themes: opportunity through inclusion and economic advancement for associates, suppliers, supply-chain workers, and communities; sustainability through responsible sourcing, labor protections, women’s empowerment, safer products, emissions cuts, nature protection, and waste reduction, including zero operational emissions by 2040 and Project Gigaton’s one-billion-ton value-chain goal by 2030; community support through affordable products, disaster relief, volunteering, grants, and cohesion efforts; and ethics and integrity to foster trust. Walmart periodically updates ESG disclosures online, which are not incorporated into its SEC filings.

nodes.title: Human Capital Management
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its 2.1 million-person global workforce and its strategy to invest in associates through four priorities: belonging, well-being, growth and digital. Belonging efforts include diversity reporting, equitable opportunities and pay practices, and multiple feedback channels. Well-being investments include competitive wages and extensive benefits, with further details in ESG reporting and financial-statement notes. Growth initiatives offer career pathways, training and education, including Walmart Academy and Live Better U. Digital tools aim to improve productivity, engagement and associate experience, alongside real-time feedback apps and free virtual medical and mental health care for eligible U.S. plan members.

nodes.title: Information About Our Executive Officers
nodes.summary: The text lists Walmart’s ten executive officers as of the 10-K filing, noting that each is appointed by and serves at the Board’s pleasure and that the stated experience generally reflects the prior five years. For each officer, it gives name, current title and effective date, prior roles and employers, year the current position began, and age. The officers span corporate affairs, legal and governance, finance and accounting, U.S. and international operations, technology, people, and Sam’s Club leadership.

nodes.title: Our Website and Availability of SEC Reports and Other Information
nodes.summary: Walmart’s website provides free access, as soon as reasonably practicable after SEC submission, to its SEC filings and shareholder documents; the SEC’s website also hosts electronic issuer filings. Walmart’s filings, senior financial officers’ reporting protocols, and Code of Conduct are online and available in print upon request from Investor Relations. Substantive amendments or waivers to the protocols or the CEO’s, CFO’s, or controller’s Code of Conduct are disclosed in the website’s Corporate Governance section for 12 months.

summary: Walmart’s business overview covers its history, omnichannel strategy, scale, fiscal 2024 results, operations and three reportable segments: Walmart U.S., Walmart International and Sam’s Club. It describes each segment’s markets, formats, merchandise, memberships, services, technology, sales, competition, seasonality, distribution and fulfillment, alongside intellectual property, suppliers, supply-chain factors and regulatory exposure. It also outlines ESG priorities, associate workforce and development, executive officers, and access to SEC filings, governance materials and conduct policies.

title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS

nodes.title: Strategic Risks Failure to successfully execute our omni-channel strategy and the cost of our investments in eCommerce and technology may materially adversely affect our market position, net sales and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The filing warns that listed risks are not exhaustive and could materially harm the company’s business, operations, financial position, and liquidity. It highlights the risk that an evolving retail market and growing digital shopping may outpace the company’s omni-channel strategy. Investments in eCommerce, AI and other technology, talent, automation, acquisitions, partnerships, store remodels, and customer initiatives may fail to drive growth or offset slower store expansion. Success depends on delivering a seamless customer experience; execution failures or reputational declines could weaken market position and sales and trigger asset impairments. More online grocery and eCommerce sales may reduce store traffic and cross-selling. Investment costs and operating losses may hurt near-term results, while failure to realize benefits could harm longer-term performance.

nodes.title: If we do not timely identify or effectively respond to consumer trends or preferences, it could negatively affect our relationship with our customers, demand for the products and services we sell, our market share and the growth of our business.
nodes.summary: Failure to anticipate changing consumer preferences, spending, and shopping patterns could weaken customer relationships, demand, market share, and growth. Forecasting errors in merchandise, inventory, pricing, or promotions can cause lower sales, spoilage, markdowns, excess or insufficient stock, service disruptions, and higher costs. Success depends on relevant customer data, suitable assortments, inventory management, and competitive pricing, while customers increasingly value transparency, experience, convenience, and shipping. Negative publicity or incidents involving the company, its workforce, theft, or business partners may damage trust, trigger boycotts, unrest, investigations, lost sales, terminated relationships, and recruiting or retention difficulties. Growing fulfillment and technology networks are harder to operate, and effective performance is not assured.

nodes.title: We face strong competition from other retailers, wholesale club operators, omni-channel retailers and other businesses which could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company faces intense, evolving competition across physical, eCommerce and omni-channel retail and related services, including from new, well-funded or more innovative businesses. Competitors vie for customers, employees, digital visibility, products and services. Competition spans price, assortment, availability, service, locations, convenience, shopping experience, digital platforms, and delivery cost, speed and options. Failure to respond to market shifts, competitors’ innovations or execution challenges could harm financial performance. Industry consolidation, alliances, bankruptcies or reduced operations may create stronger competitors with greater resources, merchandise access, reach and broader offerings at competitive prices, also posing financial risks.

nodes.title: General or macro-economic factors, both domestically and internationally, may materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks to financial performance from domestic and international economic conditions, including inflation, interest rates, energy and other costs, unemployment, credit and consumer spending changes, taxes, regulation, trade barriers, and recession. These may reduce demand, lower margins, slow inventory turnover, increase markdowns and expenses, impair assets, and raise supplier costs or limit supply. Strategic alliances and investments may underperform or harm competitiveness. Pandemics can disrupt demand, staffing, inventory, supply chains, operations, and finances, while intensifying other risks. Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical conflict, terrorism, civil unrest, violence, and theft may damage or close facilities, disrupt transport, staffing, digital access, and consumer behavior.

nodes.title: Economic, Alliance, and Pandemic Risks
key_items: The performance of strategic alliances and other business relationships to support the expansion of our business could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
Operational Risks Global or regional health pandemics or epidemics, such as COVID-19, could negatively impact our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: Economic conditions can raise operating and sales costs, harm suppliers’ capacity or increase their costs, and reduce product margins. Strategic alliances and other business relationships may underperform expectations, weaken competitiveness, or harm financial results through related investments. Pandemics and other health crises can disrupt demand, inventory, supply chains, operations, costs, and financial performance amid uncertain restrictions, economic effects, and recovery; they may also intensify risks involving consumer behavior, competition, reputation, initiatives, cybersecurity, payments, technology, labor, litigation, and regulation.

nodes.title: Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical events, catastrophic and other events could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Natural disasters, severe weather, climate change, geopolitical conflict, violence, theft, and other catastrophic events may damage or close stores, clubs, and facilities; disrupt staffing, customer access, digital platforms, infrastructure, communications, supply, transport, and product availability; and reduce consumer income or spending while raising procurement, transport, energy, and compliance costs. Climate-related physical and transition risks may affect facilities, commodities, communities, markets, and stakeholder perceptions. The company bears resulting property, inventory, and interruption losses; impacts, especially those concentrated in the U.S., could materially harm operations and financial performance. Hurricane Otis is cited as a fiscal 2024 example that was not materially significant.

nodes.title: Risks associated with our suppliers could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company relies on diverse domestic and international suppliers, making reliable global sourcing essential to financial performance. Suppliers must comply with laws and company standards, but finding qualified suppliers and obtaining sufficient products efficiently—especially overseas—is challenging. Risks beyond the company’s control include political, economic, pandemic-related and financial disruptions; suppliers’ capacity, compliance, labor, indemnification, raw-material, safety and quality problems; shipping delays, shortages, costs, security and currency fluctuations; inflation; and trade policies, tariffs, sanctions, and import/export restrictions. These factors may disrupt operations and materially harm financial performance.

nodes.title: If the quality or safety of products we sell in stores or online fails to meet our customers' expectations or regulatory standards, we could lose customers, incur liability for any injuries caused by a product we sell or otherwise experience a material impact to our brand, reputation and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from poor quality or unsafe products sold directly or through third-party marketplaces, including customer loss, injuries and liability, recalls or regulatory enforcement, reputational and financial harm, and difficulty recovering indemnification or damages from suppliers and sellers. Marketplace responsibility and compliance obligations remain legally uncertain despite controls. It also warns that information-system outages, cyberattacks, disasters, errors, and technology upgrades could disrupt operations, corrupt data, raise costs, weaken financial controls, or prevent anticipated benefits. Finally, it introduces reliance on online shopping and omni-channel technologies, whose failures could harm results and global growth.

nodes.title: Product Marketplace and Information-System Risks
key_items: If the quality or safety of products offered for sale on our third-party marketplace fails to meet our customers' expectations or regulatory standards, we could be held directly liable, lose customers, become subject to regulatory enforcement or otherwise experience reputational harm.

We rely extensively on information and financial systems to process transactions, summarize results and manage our business. Disruptions in our systems could harm our ability to conduct our operations.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from unsafe or poor-quality products sold directly or through third-party marketplaces, including liability, regulatory action, customer and reputational harm, counterfeit or infringing goods, and sellers’ inability to indemnify or pay damages. It also explains dependence on business-critical information and financial systems, potential disruptions from cyberattacks, disasters, errors, and outages, the costs and operational impacts of failures, risks from system upgrades, and possible adverse effects of a financial-system upgrade on controls and business performance.

nodes.title: If the technology-based systems that give our customers the ability to shop with us online and enable us to deliver products and services do not function effectively, our operating results, as well as our ability to grow our omni-channel business globally, could be materially adversely affected.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks to Walmart’s omnichannel and e-commerce strategy if its digital platforms, technology, supply chain systems, or third-party services fail to meet customer expectations, causing lost sales, reputational harm, weaker growth, and adverse results. It details extensive cybersecurity and privacy threats to customer, member, employee, vendor, payment, and health information, including attacks, system vulnerabilities, human error, third-party breaches, detection and response challenges, and operational or supply-chain disruption. Potential consequences include service outages, data misuse, litigation, regulatory action, fines, remediation costs, liability, and damage to reputation, competitiveness, financial performance, and strategy. It also covers payment-card security standards and liabilities, financial-service compliance obligations, privacy laws, and breach-notification requirements.

nodes.title: Changes in third-party reimbursements and contracts, type or scope of offerings of our health and wellness business or the Walmart Health business could adversely affect our overall results of operations, cash flows and liquidity.
nodes.summary: Walmart’s U.S., Sam’s Club and international pharmacy operations, Walmart Health centers, telehealth service and UnitedHealth Group collaboration face risks from reimbursement and contract changes, payer mix and formularies, network participation, drug costs and supply disruptions, competition, regulation, economic conditions, customer affordability, staffing, technology, public health and evolving care practices. These factors could reduce pharmacy sales and margins, health-service volumes and reimbursement, limit expansion and cross-selling, and ultimately harm overall operating results, cash flows and liquidity.

nodes.title: Our failure to attract and retain qualified associates, increases in wage and benefit costs, changes in laws and other labor issues could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text warns that difficulty attracting and retaining qualified associates, labor shortages and competition, rising wages and benefit or insurance costs, labor-law changes, and unsuccessful organizational or leadership transitions could harm service and financial performance. It also notes that missing high market expectations for sales, operating income, growth, eCommerce, higher-margin initiatives, capital spending, comparable sales, or earnings—or changes to dividends, buybacks, taxes, analyst estimates, or relative retail performance—could lower the stock price and increase volatility.

nodes.title: Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates may materially adversely affect our financial performance and our reported results of operations.
nodes.summary: Unfavorable currency movements can reduce Walmart’s reported international and consolidated results through translation of foreign operations and higher costs for products bought in other currencies, especially when selling prices cannot be raised. International operations, which generated about 18% of fiscal 2024 sales across numerous regions, face political, economic, legal, regulatory, tax, trade, currency, labor, competition, product-safety, environmental, data-protection, and other country-specific risks. Sanctions, trade restrictions, geopolitical conflict, inflation, devaluation, operational complexity, tax issues, and weaker intellectual-property enforcement may disrupt business, finances, or reputation. Associates, contractors, or agents may also violate anti-corruption or sanctions laws despite company policies and compliance programs, exposing Walmart to penalties and reputational harm.

nodes.title: Changes in tax and trade laws, regulations and interpretations could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Walmart warns that tax and trade-law changes, tariffs, and regulations could raise sourcing costs and selling prices, harming its business and financial performance; its U.S. segments generated about 82% of fiscal 2024 sales. Tax estimates depend on judgments about worldwide earnings, deferred taxes, laws, rates, accounting rules, interpretations, and transfer pricing. New or retroactive requirements may raise compliance costs or outpace system readiness. The Tax Act, OECD Pillar Two’s 15% minimum tax, and other international reforms may affect its effective tax rate. Audits and changing rules could make final tax outcomes differ materially from recorded amounts, affecting earnings and cash flows.

nodes.title: Changes in and/or failure to comply with other laws, regulations and interpretations of such laws and regulations specific to the businesses and jurisdictions in which we operate could materially adversely affect our reputation, market position or our business and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company faces extensive and changing U.S. and international regulation, especially in healthcare and pharmacy (licensing, controlled substances, reimbursement, billing, fraud and abuse, practitioner standards and health-data rules), as well as competition, environmental, product, trade, financial-services, labor, sanctions and ESG requirements. Drug-pricing and healthcare reforms, financial-services oversight, and evolving privacy and cybersecurity laws—including HIPAA, CCPA, GDPR and China’s PIPL—may require operational changes and substantial compliance costs, and carry penalties. Regulatory scrutiny, audits, investigations, litigation and challenges may damage reputation or restrict business. Noncompliance or ineffective responses could lead to fines, criminal or civil sanctions, lost licenses or government-program participation, suspended payments, terminated relationships, operational limits, and material harm to business and financial performance.

nodes.title: We are subject to risks related to litigation and other legal proceedings that may materially adversely affect our results of operations, financial position and liquidity.
nodes.summary: The company faces extensive litigation, regulatory investigations, audits and possible indemnification obligations that could materially harm its financial results, position or liquidity. Matters include wage-and-hour and consumer class actions; opioid investigations and lawsuits, with a $3.3 billion settlement liability mostly paid in fiscal 2024 but remaining claims unpredictable; alleged Indian foreign-investment and Mexican competition violations; and FTC/DOJ matters concerning money-transfer services, fraud prevention and anti-money-laundering compliance. Outcomes and potential losses are often uncertain. The bylaws designate Delaware’s Court of Chancery as the exclusive forum for specified shareholder claims, potentially raising costs or limiting forum choice; unenforceability could increase litigation costs. Federal securities-law jurisdiction is unaffected.

nodes.title: Our reputation may be adversely affected if we are not able to satisfy varied stakeholder expectations with respect to our ESG goals.
nodes.summary: The company’s reputation, public perception, associate morale, and customer or shareholder support could suffer if it fails—or is perceived to fail—to meet ESG goals or evolving, diverse stakeholder expectations. It sets and reports on ESG priorities, strategies, initiatives, and progress, including climate initiatives, but cannot guarantee success; outcomes depend on risks and uncertainties, many outside its control. Stakeholders may also be dissatisfied with its goals or efforts. ESG reporting discusses related challenges but is not incorporated into or part of the Form 10-K.

summary: The section warns that numerous risks could materially harm Walmart’s business, operations, financial position, liquidity, or reputation. These include execution and costs of omni-channel, eCommerce, technology, and growth initiatives; changing consumer preferences, competition, forecasting, and reputation; macroeconomic, pandemic, climate, disaster, geopolitical, supplier, product-safety, information-system, cybersecurity, privacy, and payment risks; pharmacy, healthcare, reimbursement, and labor challenges; foreign exchange and international operations; tax, trade, and other regulatory changes; litigation and investigations; and failure to meet varied stakeholder expectations for ESG goals.

title: ITEM 1C. CYBERSECURITY
key_items: Board of Directors' oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats; Management's role in assessing and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats
Board of Directors' oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats
Management's role in assessing and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats
Protecting our technology and information systems; Incident response and recovery planning; Third-party risk management; Training and awareness
Protecting our technology and information systems
summary: Walmart frames cybersecurity around digital trust and enterprise risk management, using cross-functional measures to protect operations and information. The Board delegates cybersecurity oversight to the Audit Committee, which receives management updates and escalations. The CISO leads the program, supported by multidisciplinary teams and the CTO. Guided by NIST standards, the program covers system safeguards and monitoring, incident response and recovery, third-party risk, recurring training, and periodic internal and external assessments and testing. Some Walmart and provider systems have experienced threats or incidents, but none are known to have materially affected or be likely to materially affect the company; future incidents remain possible, and related risks are discussed in Item 1A.

title: ITEM 2. PROPERTIES
summary: As of January 31, 2024, the document reports retail unit counts and square footage for Walmart U.S., Sam’s Club, International, and the total company, with International figures generally dated December 31, 2023, except Canada. It also details owned and leased retail units and distribution facilities, including fulfillment and returns facilities; some facilities are third-party operated. The company describes its owned and leased offices and store land, independent building contractors, lease rental and escalation terms, renewal options, and refers readers to segment distribution disclosures.

title: ITEM 3. LEGAL PROCEEDINGS
summary: The Company describes ordinary-course litigation and government investigations, referring to its financial-statement contingencies note and listing case details. Opioid matters include a two-county trial judgment imposing about $0.7 billion jointly over 15 years plus injunctions, now under appeal with questions before Ohio’s Supreme Court; other MDL and nationwide cases continue. A settlement framework covering substantially all state, local, and tribal claims became effective in September 2023, with substantially all related accrued amounts paid by January 2024. In DOJ litigation, some distribution and dispensing claims were dismissed, while one dispensing theory remains. Related derivative and securities class actions involve oversight and disclosures; some are stayed, a court dismissed distribution-practices claims, an independent committee is investigating, and a class-action dismissal motion is pending. Other listed proceedings concern ASDA equal-value employment claims, money-transfer services, and a Mexico antitrust investigation.

title: II. CERTAIN OTHER MATTERS:
key_items: III. ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS; ITEM 4. MINE SAFETY DISCLOSURES
summary: The text describes a July 2021 Indian Foreign Direct Investment show-cause notice to Flipkart and others over alleged 2009–2015 violations, before Walmart’s 2018 majority acquisition. Flipkart is responding and intends to defend itself; proceedings and potential penalties remain uncertain, with no material impact currently expected but no assurance. It also covers a California suit filed in December 2021 over allegedly hazardous waste management, set for trial September 30, 2024, and an EPA October 2023 Clean Air Act violation finding concerning refrigeration leak detection and repair. Walmart is defending/cooperating, outcomes and possible penalties are uncertain, and no material impact is currently expected. Mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

nodes.title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS (intro)
nodes.summary: The MD&A explains its purpose, fiscal years covered and use of segment operating income, comparable sales and currency-impact measures, including calculation limits. It notes the February 2024 three-for-one stock split, strategic investments in automation, supply chain and earnings diversification, and Walmart International portfolio changes: sales of Asda and Seiyu, Massmart buyout and country exits, and increased PhonePe ownership. It describes intense omni-channel competition, factors and risks affecting results, fiscal 2024 inflation and pricing/merchandising responses that may affect margins, and continued economic and operational uncertainty; segment results follow.

nodes.title: Company Performance Metrics
nodes.summary: The company’s priorities are growth, margin improvement, and stronger ROI through productivity and disciplined investment, while maintaining competitive strategies and everyday low prices and costs. Growth focuses on omnichannel shopping, comparable sales, membership, Walmart+, and eCommerce. The text defines comparable sales, distinguishes fiscal-calendar figures from retail-calendar reporting, and explains the focus on U.S. results. U.S. comparable sales including fuel rose 4.9% in fiscal 2024 versus 8.2% in 2023; Walmart U.S. rose 5.5% and 7.0%, respectively. Fiscal 2024 growth reflected higher transactions and average ticket, especially grocery and health and wellness; 2023 growth reflected higher average tickets, food sales, and inflation.

nodes.title: Growth
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks affecting results, including economic, climate, health, supply-chain, labor, regulatory, and cybersecurity factors, with further detail in the company’s Risk Factors. It describes inflation’s effects on fiscal 2024 merchandise costs and pricing and sourcing strategies that may affect gross margin, plus continued economic uncertainty. Financial priorities are growth, margin improvement, and returns; growth centers on omnichannel shopping, membership, eCommerce, and comparable sales. It defines comparable sales and explains fiscal 2024/2023 results: U.S. sales rose 4.9%/8.2%, Walmart U.S. 5.5%/7.0%, and Sam’s Club 2.3%/14.6%, driven by transactions, average ticket, category trends, and eCommerce pickup and delivery.

nodes.title: Margin
nodes.summary: The company prioritizes margin growth through productivity, technology and process improvements, cost and inventory management, expense discipline, and a business mix emphasizing higher-margin advertising and membership; it defines operating income leverage as operating income growing faster than net sales. Fiscal 2024 net sales were $642.637 billion versus $605.881 billion in 2023. Gross profit rates were 23.7% and 23.5%, respectively, rising 27 basis points in 2024 due mainly to Walmart U.S. pricing and lower markdowns, partly offset by lower-margin product mix, after falling 98 basis points in 2023 because of U.S. markdowns and mix, supply-chain costs, and Sam’s Club LIFO inflation charges. Operating expenses as a share of sales fell 60 basis points in 2024, partly by lapping prior-year opioid settlement and International restructuring charges ($3.3 billion and $0.8 billion); they rose 23 basis points in 2023, with those charges partly offset by sales growth and lower incremental COVID costs. Operating income was $27.012 billion (4.2% of sales) in 2024 and $20.428 billion (3.4%) in 2023; operating margin rose 83 basis points in 2024 and declined 120 basis points in 2023, reflecting the factors described.

nodes.title: Returns
key_items: Return on Assets and Return on Investment
nodes.summary: Walmart expects returns on capital to improve and measures them through ROA, ROI and free cash flow, alongside shareholder returns from repurchases and dividends. Fiscal 2024 ROA rose to 6.6% from 4.6% in 2023, mainly due to higher net and operating income. ROI increased to 15.0% from 12.7%, reflecting improved operating income and business performance, partly offset by greater invested capital. The text explains ROI’s non-GAAP definition, calculation, differences from GAAP ROA, limitations, and presents reconciliations, formulas, and related balance-sheet data for fiscal 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: Strategic Capital Allocation
nodes.summary: Walmart prioritizes capital spending on higher-return automation, eCommerce, supply chain, technology, and store and club investments; tables detail fiscal 2024 and 2023 allocations. The text defines free cash flow (operating cash flow less property and equipment payments) as a non-GAAP supplemental measure, reports results for fiscal 2022–2024, and explains year-over-year changes through operating cash flows, working capital, payment timing, opioid charges, and increased capital expenditures. It notes limitations, cautions that companies calculate the measure differently, and reconciles free cash flow to operating cash flow alongside investing and financing cash flows.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
Consolidated Results of Operations
nodes.summary: The text reports Walmart’s consolidated results for fiscal 2024–2022, including revenues, net sales, comparable sales, gross profit, operating income, debt-extinguishment losses, other gains/losses, net income, store counts and retail square footage, with a note on which locations are counted. It explains revenue and sales growth drivers, gross-margin and operating-expense changes, investment-related losses, prior debt retirements, and tax-rate fluctuations, including PhonePe’s separation. Consolidated net income was $16.3 billion in 2024 and $11.3 billion in 2023; diluted EPS was $1.91, $1.42 and $1.62 in 2024, 2023 and 2022.

nodes.title: Walmart U.S. Segment
nodes.summary: Walmart U.S. results for fiscal 2022–2024 report net sales, comparable-sales growth, operating income and margin, store counts, and retail square footage. Net sales rose 5.1% in fiscal 2024 and 6.9% in 2023, chiefly due to comparable-sales increases of 5.5% and 7.0%. Fiscal 2024 growth reflected more transactions and higher average tickets, especially in grocery and health and wellness; 2023 growth reflected higher tickets, food sales, inflation, and transactions. E-commerce, mainly pickup and delivery, contributed 2.6% and 0.7% to comparable sales, respectively. Gross profit rate rose 20 basis points in 2024 due to price management and lower markdowns, partly offset by lower-margin mix; it fell 85 basis points in 2023 due to markdowns, mix, and supply-chain costs, partly offset by inflation-related pricing. Operating expenses as a share of sales rose 9 basis points in 2024 due to variable pay, but fell 25 basis points in 2023 due to sales growth and lower COVID-related costs, partly offset by wages. Operating income increased $1.5 billion in 2024 and declined $1.0 billion in 2023.

Gross margin rose 20 basis points in 2024 through supply-chain efficiencies, partly offset by format/channel shifts; it fell 50 basis points in 2023 due to lower-margin mix. Operating expenses as a share of sales fell 152 basis points in 2024 as restructuring charges lapsed and sales grew, after rising 41 basis points in 2023 due to those charges. Operating income increased $1.9B in 2024 and declined $0.8B in 2023.

nodes.title: Sam's Club Segment

Excluding-fuel figures help investors and management assess performance amid fuel-price volatility. In 2024 and 2023, sales rose 2.2% and 14.7%, driven by comparable-sales growth, transactions, average ticket, grocery and health and wellness; eCommerce contributed 1.7% and 0.8%, while 2024 fuel deflation partly offset growth. Gross margin rose 55 basis points in 2024 as prior-year markdowns lapsed, but fell 155 basis points in 2023 amid markdowns, costs, and LIFO inflation charges. Membership income grew 7.5% and 7.0%, supported by membership and Plus growth. Expense ratios rose 46 basis points in 2024 due to lower fuel sales and technology spending, and fell 97 basis points in 2023 due to higher sales. Operating income increased $0.2 billion in 2024 and decreased $0.3 billion in 2023.

2005 Indenture Covenants and Corporate Transactions
key_items: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The 2005 Indenture permits debt securities to be issued in unlimited amounts and additional similar securities to be combined into an existing series without holder consent; New York law governs. Its limited covenants do not restrict debt or lease obligations, liens, or dividends and stock repurchases. The company may merge, consolidate, reorganize, or transfer substantially all assets if a U.S.-organized successor assumes its obligations, no continuing default exists, and other conditions are met. nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: The indenture defines defaults as overdue interest (uncured for 30 days), unpaid principal or premium, uncured covenant or warranty breaches (90 days after written notice), bankruptcy, insolvency or reorganization, and series-specific designated events; a default for one series need not affect others. Continuing defaults generally permit the trustee or holders of 25% of a series to accelerate its debt, while bankruptcy-related defaults automatically accelerate all series. A majority may rescind acceleration if specified conditions are met. The issuer must report annually on defaults. Individual holders may bring proceedings only after meeting notice, request, indemnity and waiting-period requirements, subject to majority direction and equal treatment. A series majority can direct remedies and waive certain defaults; the trustee must act prudently. Each holder retains an unimpaired right to sue for payment when due.

nodes.title: Events of Default and Waiver

Mergers or asset transfers without holder consent are allowed if specified successor, U.S. organization, no-default, and other conditions are met; the indenture imposes no limits on additional debt, liens, or sale-leasebacks. nodes.title: Payment on the 2.550% 2026 Notes
nodes.summary: Payments of principal, redemption amounts, accrued interest, and additional amounts on the 2.550% 2026 Notes are payable in euros. If euros become unavailable or cease to be used for specified monetary or settlement purposes, payments switch to U.S. dollars until euros are available or used again. Conversion uses the Federal Reserve’s mandated rate, or otherwise the latest Wall Street Journal euro-dollar rate, as of the second Business Day before payment. Dollar payment does not constitute default under the notes or 2005 Indenture. A Business Day excludes weekends, New York City or London bank-closing days, and days when TARGET2 or its successor is closed.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: Payments on the 2.550% 2026 Notes are generally made without U.S. tax withholding; if withholding is legally required, the issuer pays additional amounts so eligible Non-U.S. beneficial owners receive the net amount they would have received without withholding. Additional amounts are excluded for specified U.S. connections, late presentation, certain taxes and entity statuses, non-withholding taxes, avoidable paying-agent withholding, failure to provide required tax documentation (including FATCA), certain shareholders and controlled foreign corporations, EU savings-tax withholding, and combinations of these exceptions. nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons

Redemption requires 30–60 days’ prior notice and is at 100% of principal plus accrued and unpaid interest through the redemption date.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem the 2.550% 2026 Notes in whole or in part at any time. Before January 8, 2026, the price is the greater of par or the present value of remaining principal and interest payments (excluding accrued interest), discounted using Actual/Actual (ICMA) at the Comparable Government Bond Rate plus 15 basis points, plus accrued interest through but excluding redemption. On or after that date, redemption is at par plus accrued interest. Interest installments due on or before redemption remain payable to holders of record on the relevant date. Deferred bonuses are credited to the Plan Year’s Deferral Account and allocated to a Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Account under Section 3.5.

nodes.title: 3.3 Deferred Special Bonuses.
nodes.summary: Eligible Officers may defer all or part of a Special Bonus using Plan Administrator-approved forms, provided the election does not reduce payments below required tax, insurance, or other permitted withholdings. Elections are effective when received and allowed only for qualifying bonuses: (1) bonuses requiring at least 13 months of continued service, with no earlier vesting for good-reason termination or retirement, and meeting Code Section 409A rules, elected within 30 days of obtaining a binding right; or (2) bonuses specified as deferrable in a written, pre-employment offer letter referencing the Plan, elected before any services begin. Deferred amounts are credited to the officer’s Deferral Account and allocated to a Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Account under Section 3.5.

nodes.title: 3.4 Employer Matching Contribution Credits.
nodes.summary: An employer matching credit is made for a Plan Year if the participant remains employed by the employer or a related affiliate through year-end, has no separation during that year, and received deferral credits. The match equals deferred compensation and deferred MIP bonus credited for the year, capped at 6% of Excess Compensation, excluding deferrals withdrawn under Section 5.5; it is allocated to a Retirement Account under Section 3.5. Matching accounts and earnings vest after three Years of Participation, or earlier upon death before separation or disability. Distribution under Article V requires vesting as of separation.

nodes.title: 3.5 Account Allocation Elections
nodes.summary: Participants must allocate each deferred compensation, MIP bonus, or Special Bonus to a Retirement or Scheduled In-Service Account when electing deferral; related employer matching credits must be allocated to a Retirement Account. On the first allocation to a Retirement Account, they designate a permitted distribution form; on the first allocation to a Scheduled In-Service Account, they designate its Scheduled Pay Date. If no allocation is elected, the same category’s most recent prior-year allocation is reused. If none exists, pre-February 1, 2021 amounts go to the applicable existing Retirement Account(s), or a deemed permitted Retirement Account with lump-sum payment; amounts for Plan Years beginning on or after that date go to a deemed Retirement Account in the applicable year’s Class Account, also with lump-sum payment.

nodes.title: 3.6 Irrevocability of Deferral Elections and Account Allocation Elections.
nodes.summary: Deferral and account-allocation elections generally become irrevocable after their applicable filing deadline or election date; elections do not carry over to later Plan Years, so a new election is required. Officer compensation elections end upon separation but cover the last regular paycheck and are reinstated if rehired in the same Plan Year; bonus elections remain applicable to the relevant bonus despite separation or same-period rehiring. Loss of officer status ends compensation elections the following January 31, with reduced compensation prorated; short-term disability reductions also require proration. Loss of participant status ends Section 3.2 bonus elections for performance periods beginning the next calendar year, while Section 3.3 elections continue after loss of officer status. Unpaid leave suspends Section 3.1 elections, which resume upon same-year return; applicable compensation paid during leave remains subject to election, and Sections 3.2 and 3.3 elections are unaffected.

nodes.title: 3.7 Automatic Suspension of Deferral Elections.
nodes.summary: If a participant seeks an unforeseeable-emergency distribution or requests cancellation of deferrals, and the Plan Administrator or delegate determines stopping deferrals may relieve the emergency, some or all deferral elections under Sections 3.1–3.3 for that Plan Year will be cancelled as soon as administratively practicable.

Deferrals and bonuses are credited after they otherwise would be paid; matching credits are posted at year-end, with timing differing before versus from February 1, 2023. Accounts are maintained until benefits are fully paid and valued monthly. Pre-investment balances earn either monthly compounded interest by default or deemed investment gains and losses through an irrevocable election during Administrator-set windows; post-investment balances track selected investment options. The Administrator sets election procedures, and Walmart need not actually invest funds.

nodes.title: ARTICLE V. PAYMENT OF PLAN BENEFITS
5.1 Scheduled In-Service Benefits.
nodes.summary: Each Scheduled In-Service Account is paid as a lump sum within 90 days after its Scheduled Pay Date, valued on that date. If, before that date, an event triggers an earlier distribution under Section 5.2 or 5.3, the account is distributed under the applicable section instead.

nodes.title: 5.2 Separation Benefits.
nodes.summary: Upon separation from service, Scheduled In-Service Accounts are paid as lump sums; Retirement Accounts are paid according to the participant’s effective distribution election. Lump sums are paid within 90 days after the Separation Pay Date and valued as of the last day of the preceding month. Annual installments begin within 90 days after the first applicable January 31, unless it precedes the Separation Pay Date, and continue annually until fully paid. Interest-crediting portions are amortized in equal installments using the applicable interest rate; portions credited with investment earnings, gains, and losses are paid in substantially equal installments based on the remaining balance and payments.

nodes.title: 5.3 Death Benefits.
nodes.summary: If a participant dies before separation or benefit commencement, the account is paid under the elected lump-sum or installment form; one form applies to all beneficiaries, and absent an effective election, lump sum applies. Lump sums are paid within 90 days after the month of death and valued as of the prior month-end. Annual installments begin within 90 days of the first January 31 on or after death; later payments follow annually, calculated according to whether the account portion earns fixed interest or investment earnings, gains, and losses. If death occurs after installments begin, payments continue to the beneficiary, unless the applicable election requires the remaining balance as a lump sum. Participants may designate and update primary and contingent beneficiaries and payment shares. If none survive, default recipients are spouse, children, parents, siblings, then estate. If a beneficiary dies before full payment, benefits pass equally to surviving beneficiaries at that level, then the next level, or, if none, to that beneficiary’s default recipients in the same order.

nodes.title: 5.4 Form of Distribution.
nodes.summary: Upon separation from service, or death before separation, benefits may be paid as a lump sum, equal annual installments for up to 15 years, or—only for death benefits—a combination. Installments require a minimum $50,000 account value: individually for Pre-2021 accounts and collectively for Post-2020 accounts; otherwise payment defaults to a lump sum when the first installment would have been due. Participants may change elections under Plan Administrator procedures, subject to 12-month notice and effectiveness rules, a five-year payment delay (except death), a 20th-anniversary completion deadline, and 409A treatment of installments as one payment. Invalid changes are disregarded. Elections and Scheduled Pay Dates must be filed on approved forms with the Administrator.

nodes.title: 5.5 Distributions for Unforeseeable Emergencies.
nodes.summary: Upon written application, the Plan Administrator may, in its discretion, approve an emergency distribution to a participant or qualifying beneficiary, limited to the amount reasonably needed (including anticipated taxes and penalties) after considering insurance, asset liquidation, and stopping deferrals. Unvested matching-account balances and earnings are excluded. Distributions follow a specified order: current-year scheduled in-service accounts, current-year retirement accounts, then prorated remaining balances in those account types. For distributions before January 1, 2021, payment is suspended to the extent a deduction would be barred by Code Section 162(m), until deduction is reasonably expected to be allowed and emergency conditions remain satisfied.

nodes.title: 5.6 Distributions for Payment of Taxes.
nodes.summary: The Plan Administrator may accelerate a portion of a Participant’s benefits and pay it as a lump sum to cover FICA taxes and related income tax withholding, as well as state, local, or foreign tax obligations and related Code Section 3401 withholding on deferred Plan amounts, before those amounts are paid or made available.

nodes.title: 5.7 Reductions Arising from a Participant’s Gross Misconduct.
nodes.summary: Benefits are contingent on avoiding Gross Misconduct during employment with covered Walmart-related entities and any additional period under Walmart’s Statement of Ethics. If the Plan Administrator finds misconduct, the participant forfeits employer matching credits and related earnings; deferral-account earnings and remaining installments are recalculated using 50% of the applicable rate, but net losses are not adjusted. Deferred compensation, MIP bonuses, and special bonuses cannot be forfeited. If misconduct is found after payment, the participant or beneficiary must repay amounts exceeding the entitlement under this section.

nodes.title: ARTICLE VI. ADMINISTRATION
nodes.summary: The Plan Administrator administers the Plan and has exclusive discretion to interpret its terms, determine eligibility and benefit amounts, resolve disputes, and adopt or repeal operating rules. It may appoint assistants and establish forms. Its decisions bind affected parties, subject to Article VII’s claims procedure. For matters concerning its own Plan rights or benefits, the Committee performs these duties, and the Administrator cannot participate or vote. The Administrator may delegate or revoke responsibilities in writing; delegates’ actions have the same effect as its own, must report periodically, and the Administrator is not liable for their acts or omissions.

nodes.title: ARTICLE VII. CLAIMS PROCEDURE
nodes.summary: Claims must be filed in writing within one year after separation from service; late claims eliminate all rights to benefits. Denials must generally be decided within 60 days (up to 120 days with special circumstances) and explain the reasons, relevant Plan provisions, needed information, review procedure, and ERISA lawsuit rights. Claimants may appeal in writing within 60 days, review relevant documents, and submit comments. Appeals have similar 60/120-day deadlines and written decisions must state reasons, provisions, document-access rights, voluntary appeal procedures, and ERISA rights. Disability claims follow the cited DOL regulation.

nodes.summary: The plan allocates specified share amounts for company and open-market purchases, subject to stockholder approval. Cash payroll and voluntary contributions are capped at $125,000 annually; deduction minimums, increments, effectiveness, changes, termination, submission methods, and possible exclusion from final paychecks are specified. nodes.title: IV. Account Purchases, Maintenance & Sales
nodes.summary: The section governs account establishment, share purchases, allocations, ownership, statements, risks, fees and sales. Accounts are opened for participants and certain award recipients; contributions are invested within five business days through company-issued, treasury or market shares, with specified pricing, bundling and possible real-time trading rules. Non-U.S. contributions are converted to dollars, participants bear currency and market risks, and participation may be suspended for legal reasons. Shares are allocated proportionally, owned by participants, held in the administrator’s name, and subject to delivery, voting, transfer and pledge rules. Annual statements are provided; purchase commissions are waived, while sale and maintenance fees apply as specified. Participants may direct sales subject to insider-trading rules, receive net proceeds, and bear applicable currency-conversion risks.

nodes.title: V. Account Closure & Termination of Employment
nodes.summary: Participants stopping payroll deductions remain enrolled until their account is closed. On closure, they must receive a full distribution in stock (fractional shares paid in cash) or cash from selling all shares, subject to fees. After non-death employment termination, accounts remain open with the participant paying applicable fees. Employees transferring to a nonparticipating affiliate may keep accounts at company expense while employed there, but cannot make or receive contributions unless eligibility is restored; closure distributions follow the same options and fees. Upon death, deductions and matching contributions stop, and the account is distributed under committee rules, typically to a designated beneficiary or joint tenant, or otherwise to the estate.

nodes.title: VI. Award Program

Its Outstanding Performance component grants Stock for consistently outstanding job-related performance over a month, quarter, or year, through share certificates or shares purchased and credited to an account; awards require Committee or delegate approval and are subject to individual dollar limits.
